column2: He pierced him in the battle with seven iron arrows there; Shaineya pierced him back with gold-adorned arrows.
Then the battle was exceedingly fierce, terrifying to eyes and ears, O king, dreadful and wondrous, to be watched from all sides.
Hair stood on end for all beings there on seeing that deed in battle of Karna and Shaineya, O king.
In the meantime Drona's son went against the very mighty Parshata, subduer of foes, destroyer of enemy valour.
Drona's son, enraged, with Dhananjaya far away, said, "Stand, stand today, slayer of a Brahmana; you will not escape alive from me."
Having said this, the hero, quick-working, covered the Parshata with sharp, terrible, keen arrows, striving with all his might, the great chariot-warrior.
As Drona's son looked at the Parshata in the battle, so the Parshata, slayer of heroes, seeing Drona's son in battle, not glad at heart, thought death near for himself.
Seeing Dhrishtadyumna standing in the battle, O king of kings, Drona's son, sighing with rage, ran at the Parshata; seeing each other, the two attained supreme fury.
Then the mighty Drona's son, hastening, O lord of men, said to Dhrishtadyumna near him, "Vile Panchala, today I shall send you to death.
The sin you committed in killing Drona long ago will today fall upon you, as an unskilled act does."
If you stand unprotected by Partha in battle and do not retreat, fool, this I tell you truly.
Thus addressed, the mighty Dhrishtadyumna replied: "The reply to you will be my sword itself, by which your father, though striving in the battle, was despatched.
If I killed Drona, a Brahmana in name, why shall I not now kill you in battle by valour?"
Having said this, O great king, the commander, impatient, the Parshata, pierced Drona's son with a sharp arrow.
Then Drona's son, greatly enraged, covered the quarters in the battle with straight-jointed arrows over Dhrishtadyumna, O king.
Neither the sky nor the quarters nor the warriors were seen all around, O great king, covered by thousands of arrows.
Likewise the Parshata covered Drona's son, ornament of the battle, with arrows in the sight of the charioteer's son.
Radheya, O great king, alone held back the Panchalas with the Pandavas, the sons of Draupadi, Yudhamanyu and the great chariot-warrior Satyaki, a sight to behold on all sides.
Dhrishtadyumna in the battle cut Drona's son's bow; casting aside the cut bow, he took another swift, dreadful bow and arrows like venomous serpents.
O king of kings, he shattered the Parshata's bow, dart, mace, banner, horses, charioteer and chariot in a moment with arrows.
With his bow cut, chariotless, horses and charioteer slain, he took a great sword and a shield marked with a hundred moons, shining.

Drona's son, O king of kings, the great chariot-warrior, quick-handed and firm in weapons, also quickly cut that with broad-headed arrows in the battle while he had not yet dismounted; it was wondrous.
Dhrishtadyumna, chariotless, horses slain, bow cut, pierced in many ways by arrows and shattered by weapons, could not cross, though striving, O best of the Bharatas, the great chariot-warrior.
When Drona's son could not reach his end with arrows, O king, he cast aside his bow and hastened to the Parshata.
The speed of that great soul as he ran was like Garuda's swooping, wishing to seize the best of serpents.
At that very moment Madhava said to Arjuna, "See, Partha, how Drona's son strives greatly to kill the Parshata; he would surely kill him.
Free him, mighty-armed one, the Parshata, scorcher of foes, who has come into Drona's son's mouth as if into the mouth of death."
Having said this, O great king, the mighty Vasudeva sent the horses to where Drona's son stood.
Those moon-bright horses, urged by Keshava, seemed to drink the sky as they went on the road to Drona's son's chariot.
Seeing the two very valiant ones, Krishna and Dhananjaya, coming, the strong one made an effort to kill Dhrishtadyumna, O king.
Seeing Dhrishtadyumna being dragged, O lord of men, mighty Partha loosed arrows at Drona's son.
Those gold-adorned arrows, loosed hard from Gandiva, reached Drona's son and entered him like serpents into an anthill.
Pierced by those dreadful arrows, the mighty Drona's son, hero, tormented by Dhananjaya's arrows, mounted his chariot, and taking his excellent bow pierced Partha with arrows.
In the meantime the hero Sahadeva, O lord of men, carried the Parshata, scorcher of foes, away from the battle in his chariot.
Arjuna too, O great king, pierced Drona's son with feathered arrows; Drona's son, enraged, tormented his arms and chest.
Enraged in battle, Partha hurled at Drona's son an iron arrow like Death, like another rod of Death, at the Brahmana's shoulder.
Dazed by the force of the arrow in the battle, he sat down on his chariot-seat and let go his bow Vijaya.
Enraged, looking at Arjuna again and again, and wishing for single combat with Partha in the great battle,
leaving him as if slain, his charioteer, in haste, carried the hero, scorcher of foes, out of the battle in the chariot.
Then a great shout was raised by the victorious Panchalas, seeing the Parshata freed and Drona's son hard pressed.
Thousands of divine instruments were played, and lion-roars arose on seeing that dreadful, great marvel.
Having done so, Partha Dhananjaya said to Vasudeva, "Go to the Samshaptakas, Krishna; that is my chief task."
Then the Dasharha, hearing the Pandava's words, went on in the chariot with many banners, swift as mind and wind.
[Krishna said:] "This brother of yours, Pandava, is being swiftly pursued by mighty Dhritarashtra's sons, mighty archers, wishing to kill him, Partha.
The Panchalas, arrogant in battle, enraged, swift, follow the great soul Yudhishthira, wishing to save him.
This Duryodhana, armoured, with Partha's chariot-division, king of all the world, runs after the king,
wishing to kill the tiger among men, the strong one, with his brothers, with all those skilled in war, touching like venomous serpents.
These eager to seize him go—elephants, horses, chariots and foot-soldiers—Dhritarashtra's men after Yudhishthira, as suppliants after the best of jewels.
See, Satvata, the lord restrained and occupied by Bhima, like danavas wishing to carry off nectar from Shakra and Agni, helpless.
These, many, again hasten to the Pandava, like floods to the sea in the rainy season, great chariot-warriors,
roaring lion-roars and blowing conches, strong mighty archers, shaking their bows.
I think the son of Kunti, Yudhishthira, has gone into Death's mouth, fallen into the fire; good luck to you, Duryodhana is in his power.
So well arrayed is the army of Dhritarashtra's son, Pandava, that even Shakra, reaching the range of their arrows, would not escape.
The force of the arrows of the brave Duryodhana, Drona's son, Sharadvata and Karna could split even mountains.
Who could bear in battle the swiftly shot masses of arrows of the brave Duryodhana, enraged like Death?
The king, scorcher of foes, was made to turn away by Karna, who is strong, quick, skilled and learned in war.
Radheya is able to harass the best of the Pandavas in battle, accompanied by the brave, great-souled sons of Dhritarashtra.
As he fought thus in the battle, composed, the armour of Partha's elder brother was taken by other great chariot-warriors too.
The king is weakened by fasting, best of the Bharatas, and is established in Brahmanic strength, not in kshatriya strength, lord.
I think the great king Yudhishthira is not alive, Partha, since impatient Bhimasena endures the lion-roars
of the roaring sons of Dhritarashtra, again and again, tamer of foes, and of those blowing great conches, victorious in battle.
'Kill the Pandava Yudhishthira!' Karna is urging the mighty sons of Dhritarashtra, O best of the Bharatas.
Great chariot-warriors follow the king, covering him with nets of arrows—thick, tipped like the moon—and with the Pashupata, Partha; I deem the king afflicted and to be waited on.
As the Panchalas with the Pandavas follow him, in haste, best of all weapon-bearers, wishing to lift the strong one as if sinking into the netherworld,
the king's banner is not seen, struck down by Karna's arrows, in the sight of the twins, Partha, Satyaki and Shikhandin,
of Dhrishtadyumna, Bhima, Shatanika, and all the Panchalas and Chedis, O Bharata.
This Karna, Partha, in battle shatters the Pandava army with arrows, like an elephant a lotus-pond.
These chariot-warriors of yours flee, O joy of Pandu; see, see, Partha, how these great chariot-warriors go.
These elephants, O Bharata, struck by Karna in battle, make cries of distress and flee in all ten directions.
See, Partha, throngs of fleeing chariots all around, being routed in battle by Karna, scorcher of foes.
See the elephant-rope banner of Karna the charioteer's son, best of banner-bearers, ranging here and there.
There runs Radheya towards Bhimasena's chariot, scattering hundreds of arrows and slaying your army.
See these Panchalas routed by the great soul, being slain in the great battle as Shakra the daityas.
This Karna, having conquered the Panchalas, Pandavas and Srinjayas in battle, looks in all directions, I think, for your sake.
See him drawing the excellent bow, Partha; he shines well, having conquered his foes, like Shakra surrounded by hosts of gods.
These Kauravas roar on seeing Karna's prowess, frightening the Parthas and Srinjayas by thousands in battle.
This Radheya, O giver of honour, having terrified the Pandavas with all his might in the great battle, addresses all the armies:
'Rush on, go, run fast, Kauravas, so that not one Srinjaya escapes alive from the battle.
Do so, composed; we shall go behind.' Having said so, he goes, scattering arrows from behind.
See Karna in battle, Partha, shining with a white parasol, like the sun adorning the eastern mountain.
With the parasol held over his head, shining like the full moon, O Bharata, with a hundred ribs, in the battle,
this Karna looks at you, O lord of men, with grey eyes; having made the highest effort, he will surely come into the battle.
See, mighty-armed one, how he shakes his great bow, loosing arrows like venomous serpents, the mighty one.
That Radheya is seen returning, O monkey-bannered one, coming to his own death like a moth to a lamp.
Seeing Karna alone, Dhritarashtra's son returns with a chariot-force, well prepared, wishing to protect him.
This evil-souled one with all his followers must be slain with effort by you, wishing for fame, kingdom and highest happiness.
Looking at yourself, O best of the Bharatas, as accomplished, and at Radheya who has offended the righteous Yudhishthira,
attack Radheya, the time has come immediately; holding to the noble resolve in battle, return to the leader of the chariot-hosts.
Five hundred of the chief chariots, O best of chariot-warriors, come swiftly, strong and of terrible splendour.
Five thousand elephants, twice as many horses, and ten thousands of foot-soldiers come together, Kaunteya; the army, guarding one another, advances against you.
Show yourself by yourself to the mighty-bowed charioteer's son; make the highest effort and return, O best of the Bharatas.
This Karna, in great rage, runs at the Panchalas; I see his banner towards Dhrishtadyumna's chariot; I think he will cut down the Panchalas, scorcher of foes.
I tell you something pleasing, Partha: the Kuru king, the son of Dharma, Yudhishthira, is alive.
There the mighty-armed Bhima has turned back at the head of the army, surrounded by the Srinjaya army and Satyaka's, O Bharata.
These Kauravas are being slain in battle by sharp arrows from Bhimasena and the great-souled Panchalas, Kaunteya.
The army of Dhritarashtra's son has turned away from the battle and flees swiftly, slain by Bhima's arrows.
The earth, drenched in blood like a crop destroyed, and the Bharata army, pitiable to behold, O best of the Bharatas.
See Bhimasena, lord of warriors, turned back, Kaunteya, like an enraged venomous serpent; from him the army flees.
Yellow, red, black and white banners, adorned with stars, moon and sun, and these parasols, Arjuna, are scattered.
Golden, silver and fiery banners of various kinds are being cast down, and elephants and horses scattered.
These chariot-warriors, lifeless, fall from chariots, slain by the arrows of many colours of the Panchalas, who do not flee.
The Panchalas, Dhananjaya, rush upon Dhritarashtra's strong sons, who have no men left in elephants, horses and chariots.
Relying on Bhimasena, they crush, tigers among men, giving up life, the formidable army of the enemy, tamer of foes.
These Panchalas roar and blow conches and rush on, slaying the enemy with arrows in the battle.
See, scorcher of foes, the greatness of heaven: the Panchalas, enraged, slay Dhritarashtra's men like lions elephants.
Attacked on all sides, this great army of Dhritarashtra's son is like the Ganga assailed by swift swans from Lake Manasa—by the Panchalas.
The heroes Kripa, Karna and others have exerted themselves greatly to hold back the Panchalas, like bulls among bulls.

Heroes led by Dhrishtadyumna slay the great chariot-warriors of Dhritarashtra's sons, deeply sunk in terrible weapons, by thousands; the great army of Dhritarashtra's son has mostly dejected chariots.
See, cut by Bhima's iron arrows, these elephants fall like peaks of mountains struck by the thunderbolt-wielder's bolt.
Pierced by Bhimasena's straight-jointed arrows, these great elephants flee, crushing their own divisions.
Arjuna, you do not recognise the unbearable lion-roar of Bhima roaring in battle, the victorious hero.
This Nishadi's son, on the best elephant, comes at the Pandava, enraged, javelins in hand, like Death with a rod, wishing to kill him.
As he roared, Bhima cut off both arms with their javelins, and killed him with ten sharp iron arrows like tongues of fire.
Having slain him, he comes again at other striking elephants; see him slaying, with weapon-like javelins, those dark as blue clouds, ridden by chief drivers.
Seven and seven elephants, with banners and standards, were cut by sharp arrows by Partha's elder brother, and each elephant was killed with ten iron arrows.
The roar of Dhritarashtra's men is no longer heard when the best of the Bharatas, equal to Purandara, has turned back enraged.
Three akshauhinis of Dhritarashtra's son, massed, were held back by the enraged lion among men, Bhimasena."
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing that hard deed done by Bhimasena, Arjuna destroyed the remaining enemies with sharp arrows.
Being slain in the battle, those Samshaptaka hosts, O lord, became guests of Shakra and were glad and free of sorrow.
Partha, tiger among men, with straight-jointed arrows slew the four-fold army of Dhritarashtra's son.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "When the flood of troops was fleeing without cry, again and again, what did the Kurus do? Tell me that, Sanjaya."
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing the mighty-armed Bhima, the glorious charioteer's son, his eyes red with rage, rushed at Bhimasena, O king.
Seeing your army turn from Bhimasena, the strong one with great effort rallied it, O king.
Having rallied your son's army, the mighty-armed Karna then advanced against the Pandavas, arrogant in battle.
The great chariot-warriors of the Pandavas advanced against Radheya, shaking their bows in battle and hurling arrows.
Bhimasena, Shini's grandson, Shikhandin, Janamejaya, the strong Dhrishtadyumna and all the Prabhadrakas,
and the Panchalas, tigers among men, enraged, victorious in battle, rushed at your army on every side.
Likewise your men rushed in haste at the Pandava army, great chariot-warriors wishing to kill.
Shikhandin went to Karna, and Dhrishtadyumna to your son Duhshasana, O great king, who was surrounded by a great army.
Nakula went against Vrishasena and Chitrasena, and Sahadeva against Uluka in the battle, O king.
Satyaki against Shakuni, Bhimasena against the Kauravas, and Drona's son, the great chariot-warrior, against the striving Arjuna.
Gautama (Kripa) attacked the mighty archer Yudhamanyu in the battle, and strong Kritavarman rushed at Uttamaujas.
Bhimasena alone, mighty-armed, held back all the Kurus and your sons with their divisions, O revered one.
Shikhandin, slayer of Bhishma, held back with arrows Karna as he ranged fearless, O great king.
Then Karna, stubborn, his lips trembling with rage, struck Shikhandin between the brows with three arrows.
Bearing those arrows, Shikhandin shone greatly, like a silver mountain with three peaks.
Deeply pierced by the charioteer's son in the battle, the mighty archer pierced Karna with ninety sharp arrows.
Karna killed his horses and charioteer with three arrows, and the great chariot-warrior tore down his banner with a razor-arrow.
Leaping from the chariot whose horses were slain, the scorcher of foes, enraged, hurled a dart at Karna.
Karna, cutting it in battle with three arrows, O Bharata, pierced Shikhandin with nine sharp arrows.
Avoiding the arrows loosed from Karna's bow, the best of men, best of victors, Shikhandin, swiftly withdrew.
Then Karna, O great king, scattered the Pandava armies like a mighty wind reaching a heap of cotton.
Dhrishtadyumna, afflicted by your son, struck Duhshasana in the chest with three arrows, O great king.
Duhshasana pierced his left arm, O revered one, with a sharp golden-feathered straight-jointed broad-headed arrow.
Dhrishtadyumna, pierced, impatient, sent a dreadful arrow at Duhshasana in rage, O Bharata.
Your son cut with three arrows that very swift arrow sent by Dhrishtadyumna as it came, O lord of men.
Then with seventeen other gold-adorned broad-headed arrows he reached Dhrishtadyumna and tormented his arms and chest.
Then the enraged Parshata cut his bow, O revered one, with a very sharp razor-arrow, and the people shouted.
Then, taking another bow, your son, O best of the Bharatas, surrounded Dhrishtadyumna on every side with masses of arrows.
Seeing that prowess of your great-souled son, the warriors laughed, as did the siddhas and the hosts of apsarases.
Then a dreadful battle began between your men and the enemy, dreadful, terrifying at the time of death, O scorcher of foes.
Vrishasena, piercing Nakula with five iron arrows, pierced him as he stood near his father with three more.
Nakula, enraged, smiling as it were, pierced Vrishasena firmly in the heart with a very sharp iron arrow.
Deeply pierced by the strong foe, the tormentor of foes pierced his foe with twenty and he him with five arrows.
Then with a thousand arrows those two best of men covered each other, and then the army broke.
Seeing the army of Dhritarashtra's son fleeing, the charioteer's son forcibly checked it, running after it, O lord of men; when Karna had turned back, Nakula went to the Kauravas.
Karna's son, leaving Nakula in the battle, swiftly guarded Radheya's wheel, O revered one.
Uluka, enraged in the battle, held back by Sahadeva, had his four horses killed by the mighty Sahadeva, who sent his charioteer to Yama's abode.
Uluka, leaping from the chariot, O lord of men, went to the Trigarta army, delight of his father.
Satyaki, piercing Shakuni with twenty sharp arrows, cut the banner of Subala's son with a broad-headed arrow, laughing as it were.
Subala's son, enraged in battle, O mighty king, splitting his armour, again cut his golden banner.
Then Satyaki pierced him back with sharp arrows, and tormented his charioteer with three, O great king, and swiftly sent his horses to Yama's abode with arrows.
Then, leaping suddenly, Shakuni, O best of the Bharatas, quickly mounted Uluka's chariot, and Uluka swiftly carried him away from the warrior Shaineya.
Satyaki in the battle, O king, rushed with speed at your army, and then the division broke.
Driven by Shaineya's arrows, the army, O lord of men, fled in the ten directions and fell as if lifeless.
Your son held back Bhimasena in the battle, but Bhima in a moment made that lord of the world chariotless, horseless and bannerless, and the charanas were pleased.
Then the king withdrew out of Bhimasena's range, and the whole Kuru army rushed at Bhimasena; a great shout arose there from those wishing to kill Bhima alone.
Yudhamanyu, piercing Kripa, quickly cut his bow; then Kripa, best of weapon-bearers, took another bow.
He felled Yudhamanyu's banner, charioteer and parasol to the ground, and the great chariot-warrior Yudhamanyu withdrew in the same chariot.
Uttamaujas suddenly covered Hardikya of terrible valour with arrows, like a cloud with rain a mountain.
Seeing the king before them, all the people, greatly agitated, wept aloud to Sanjaya, crying "Alas, O king!"
It was frequented by herds of many beasts, thronged with birds of many kinds, covered with trees and creepers of many kinds, and haunted by many beasts of prey.
The decline of age, the destruction of all my kin, the ruin of friends and companions have come upon me through fate; who else is more afflicted than I in this world?
He who had the strength of ten thousand elephants, in the world without a rival in battle, with a lion's sportive gait, wise, merciful, self-controlled and firm in vows—
[The hunter said:] "I know this; here the wise do not look at small virtues; all who are appointed are elders; these are the teachings for those at ease; therefore I shall kill this small serpent."
When far-sighted Vidura spoke thus, O son of Kunti, I, of vain mind, followed the sinful Duryodhana.
They prepared for him, as before, maireya, honey, meat, light drinks and wondrous varieties of food.
Thus said the sages, O king, deceived by those evil-minded ones, with eyes red with anger, looking at each other:
Having duly performed the final sacrifice, O best of the Bharatas, they all cast their fires into the water and set forth, bulls among men.
If these eternal heroes' worlds belong to Duryodhana, ignorant of dharma and sinful, a friend-injurer of the earth—
